claims.text: Controlled thermal exposure of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy induces precipitation of nanoscale Mg-rich intermetallic phases.
The Mg-rich precipitates form preferentially along grain boundaries or phase interfaces.
The initial alloy is a supersaturated, metastable solid solution produced by non-equilibrium processing.
The initial solid solution contains randomly distributed Mg atoms and only minor intermetallic constituents.
Thermal activation drives local diffusion and Mg segregation.
Mg segregation leads to nucleation and growth of intermetallic precipitates.
The intermetallic precipitates create micro-galvanic sites.
Precipitate-induced galvanic coupling changes localized corrosion behavior relative to the as-cast state.
Precipitate-induced changes in oxygen transport alter the nature and protectiveness of high-temperature oxide scales.
Aging at approximately 600–700 °C increases the volume fraction of Mg-rich precipitates relative to the as-cast baseline.
Aging increases the size of Mg-rich precipitates relative to the as-cast baseline.
Thermally aged samples exhibit corrosion current density or corrosion potential different from the as-cast baseline.
Thermally aged samples develop more non-uniform high-temperature oxide scales than the initial homogeneous state.
Thermal aging changes oxide-scale thickness or composition relative to the as-cast baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to Mg-containing alloys with density below 6 g/cm3 when elemental-property differences favor intermetallic formation.
The proposed mechanism is not expected in alloys that have already transformed fully to equilibrium phases after very long aging or excessively high temperatures.
